title: After Finding a Man on Death Row Innocent, a Judge Wants to Lead the Office That Tried Him
author: Piper French
content:
Jimmie “Chris” Duncan had [spent nearly 30 years on Louisiana’s death
row](https://boltsmag.org/the-human-cost-of-jeff-landrys-drive-to-resume-
executions/) when a district court judge named Alvin R. Sharp [vacated his
murder conviction](https://boltsmag.org/chris-duncan-louisiana-death-row-
conviction-set-aside/) last year. Sharp found that Duncan was innocent of the
charge that he murdered his then-girlfriend’s daughter Haley, and that
critical evidence in his case amounted to junk science, pushed by two doctors
responsible for a host of other wrongful convictions.

Now Sharp is running to lead the district attorney’s office that relentlessly
prosecuted Duncan for more than three decades: relying on the testimony of
those now-discredited doctors, fiercely opposing his efforts to prove his
innocence, and continuing to insist on his guilt even after Sharp’s ruling.

Sharp, who retired from the bench in February to launch his campaign, is
hoping to become the first Black DA of Louisiana’s Fourth Judicial District,
which covers Ouachita and Morehouse parishes in Northeast Louisiana. He is
competing against Mennon Campbell, a former local prosecutor who now works as
a criminal defense attorney. Both candidates are running as Republicans, in
line with the region’s conservative politics.

No matter who is elected in November, it will mark the end of an era: The
office was helmed for a quarter-century by Jerry Jones, the DA who prosecuted
Duncan at trial, and for the last decade by Stephen Robert Tew, Jones’
handpicked successor.

“It’s a change that’s been long past due,” Duncan told _Bolts_.

Duncan was released from prison in November 2025, and the Louisiana Supreme
Court upheld Sharp’s ruling of innocence this June. Haley’s family also now
believes strongly in Duncan’s innocence. But Tew, the outgoing DA, is now
trying to revive the case against Duncan, [recently demanding
DNA](https://radleybalko.substack.com/p/breaking-da-demands-dna-from-
chris?r=cgi7&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web) from both Duncan and Haley’s
mother Allison Statham on the grounds that “new evidence” has emerged in the
1993 case.** **

Duncan and Statham’s legal teams have both denounced Tew’s actions, and
Statham’s attorney told _Bolts_ that Statham strongly opposes new charges
against Duncan. “It's just total harassment,” said Scott Greene, Duncan’s
lawyer.

Tew has just three months left in his term, so his successor is likely to
inherit the case. But a win for Sharp, who was instrumental in Duncan’s
conviction reversal and release, may not ultimately benefit Duncan himself,
since the judge told _Bolts_ he’d have to recuse himself. It’s not clear how
Campbell would approach Duncan’s case; he didn’t respond to several requests
for an interview for this piece.

The next DA will also have to address overcrowding at the local jail, a
significant case backlog, and frustration that crime victims’ voices are being
ignored. Kevo Meredith, a local victim’s rights advocate who has investigated
several cold cases, fears that the DA’s office has “forgotten that when
elected, you work for _us_.”

“Whoever wins, I need one of them to go into this and say, ‘We’re going to fix
an office that is just extremely broken,’” Meredith said.

* * *

Sharp has a long legal pedigree in Ouachita Parish. His father, said to be the
first Black lawyer in Northeast Louisiana, was a well-known civil rights
attorney who fought cases challenging segregation and voter role purges. In
1992, when he was just 27, Sharp was appointed city prosecutor of Monroe, the
largest city in Ouachita Parish—a job he took over from his older brother, who
had left to become a judge.

As city attorney, he defended Monroe police officers in a civil rights case
brought by a Black man who had been bitten by police dogs. “I'm a Black lawyer
representing the majority white police in a police brutality case against a
Black guy,” he told _Bolts._ “You can imagine what kind of pressure that was.”
He argued in court that the officers were within the standard for reasonable
use of force, and won his case.

When Sharp joined the bench in 1996, Jerry Jones had already been the DA for
six years. Jones was a larger-than-life figure, a showman with a flair for the
spotlight.

In late 1993, the drowning death of Haley Oliveaux, gave Jones an opportunity
to seize it. Duncan was initially charged with negligent homicide. But after
Haley was examined by medical examiner Steven Hayne and dentist Michael West,
who reported that Duncan’s teeth “matched” bite marks on the toddler’s body,
Jones decided to seek the death penalty. He personally prosecuted Duncan, as
he did with any domestic violence case that included a death or serious
injury—the “headline-winning cases,” as Cameron Murray, a longtime local
defense attorney, put it.

Jones finally retired in 2016. Tew, his successor, had none of Jones’ bombast;
he is an administrator who is not in the habit of personally prosecuting the
office’s cases. Still, he continued to defend his predecessor’s conviction of
Duncan, who had always insisted on his innocence and was pursuing the post-
conviction relief process. The DA hired Jones’ longtime second in command, who
also served as one of Duncan’s trial prosecutors, to fight the case, and
rejected Sharp’s attempt to fashion a compromise that would have allowed
Duncan to plead guilty to a lower charge in exchange for time served. (The
office would not comment on its involvement in Duncan’s case, citing the open
investigation, other than to say: “the evidence will speak for itself in due
course.”)

In September 2024, Duncan got the chance to make his case in Sharp’s
courtroom, his first opportunity to present new evidence of his innocence in
court in decades. The hearing featured a series of experts who testified that
bite mark evidence has been roundly scientifically discredited in the
intervening decades, and that Hayne and West in particular have been exposed
as charlatans. The court watched a video that Duncan’s defense team had
unearthed showing West scraping a mold of Duncan’s teeth against Haley’s body,
appearing to create the marks he was supposedly identifying.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261016_000235-e1792185989811.jpg)Chris Duncan was
released in November 2025 after decades in prison (photo courtesy of Duncan).

Sharp listened carefully to the evidence and told the court he’d “learned so
much more” about bite mark evidence than he knew before. The jumpy, big-city
energy of one of Duncan’s lawyers clearly amused the judge, who at one point
laughingly admonished him: “We’re in the _South_!”

If he becomes DA, Sharp says he would set up a conviction integrity unit to
review other old cases like Duncan’s in order to identify procedural errors or
evidence of innocence. Similar units have led to exonerations in [New
Orleans](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/may/06/prosecutors-new-
orleans-mass-incarceration) and around the
[country](https://innocenceproject.org/news/philadelphia-men-exonerated-
jermal-shuler-brittingham-turner/), though [they
have](https://boltsmag.org/chicago-cook-county-conviction-review-forberg/)
often [fallen short](https://lawreview.colorado.edu/print/volume-97/the-
indelible-flaws-of-conviction-integrity-units-sarah-gottlieb/) of
expectations.

During his years on the bench, he said, “I have seen enough instances where I
was not convinced that justice was being sought first” by the prosecutor’s
office in this district, citing Duncan’s case as an example.

But, counterintuitively, Sharp’s candidacy isn’t necessarily good news for
Duncan himself. The Louisiana Supreme Court’s decision that upheld his ruling
and found Duncan factually innocent triggered a one-year deadline for the DA’s
office to file new charges, until June 2027; the office could also formally
acknowledge Duncan’s innocence at any point.

Given the pivotal role he played in the case, Sharp told _Bolts_ he would have
to recuse himself on the question of whether to bring new charges against
Duncan or put the case to bed forever. Local attorneys told _Bolts_ that the
most likely outcome would be for the case to fall into the hands of Attorney
General Liz Murrill, an ardent champion of the death penalty who has sought to
restart executions in the state since entering office in 2024.

Murrill has [championed legislation](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-limiting-
post-conviction-relief-murrill-landry/) that makes it harder for prisoners to
challenge their convictions and [argued in
court](https://www.nola.com/news/louisiana-death-penalty-liz-murrill-taylor-
porter/article_77a058c5-29b6-4044-be11-69a77b416005.html) that Louisiana
should execute death row prisoners who had not yet exhausted their appeals, a
claim which the state supreme court rejected.

Given Murrill’s record, the possibility troubles Duncan. “It’ll be a travesty
if they end up with it,” he said.

* * *

Meredith, the victim’s rights advocate who has been critical of Tew’s inaction
on a number of cold cases he’s worked to gather more information on, believes
that while the office is “actively pursuing” retrying Duncan, it is neglecting
other crimes.

“There are cases that have actual evidence that just get pushed to the back
burner, families that get pushed to the back burner,” he said.

Sharp echoed this criticism, pointing to Tew’s continued prosecution of Duncan
amidst this backlog as evidence of the office’s disordered priorities. “A case
like that, it takes a lot of time, it takes a lot of energy, it takes a lot of
resources, manpower,” he said.

Sharp was a Democrat for much of his life but switched his voter registration
to Republican a few years ago. Louisiana has been controlled since January
2024 by an all-GOP state government, led by Murrill and Governor Jeff Landry,
that has enacted a harsh and punitive agenda: [more
executions](https://boltsmag.org/the-human-cost-of-jeff-landrys-drive-to-
resume-executions/), [fewer paths for prisoners to challenge their
convictions,](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-limiting-post-conviction-relief-
murrill-landry/) [harsher youth
criminalization,](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-amendment-3-youth-
prosecution-adult-system/) [fewer chances for
parole](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-special-session-crime-jail-population-
sheriffs/).

Asked if he shares state Republicans’ vision for criminal justice, Sharp told
_Bolts_ , “If that were true, then Jimmie Duncan would probably still be at
Angola.” He added, “Alvin Sharp is his own man.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/752242420_1430869678864219_4672604170267582054_n.jpg)A
campaign sign for Mennon Campbell (photo via Campbell campaign/Facebook)

Still, both Sharp and Campbell, his opponent, have sounded broadly similar
notes by highlighting their commitment to aggressively prosecuting crime. They
also say they want to work through the office’s backlog of cases that’s
contributing to dismal conditions in the local jail, where people are held
pretrial. “There’s people sleeping on the floor,” Murray, the local defense
attorney, said.

Campbell does not have detailed campaign proposals on his
[website](https://mennoncampbell.com/#home), and did not respond to repeated
inquiries for this piece. In a recent podcast
[interview](https://www.buzzsprout.com/2535982/episodes/19523832-ep-18-mennon-
campbell-on-leadership-justice#transcript), he indicated he’d seek the maximum
charges for a repeat offender, meaning a burglar could get 24 years in prison
if it were his second felony, or life imprisonment for a third felony
conviction. “I don’t want that guy back in my community,” he said. He has not
indicated whether he would continue the attempt to prosecute Duncan if he
takes office.

Sharp said in a different podcast [hosted by
Meredith](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-election-for-da-is-
comimg/id1740451660?i=1000779363339) that he would not rule out seeking the
death penalty as DA, and pledged to enact a “no tolerance” policy for people
who commit crimes against children and the elderly.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/820525979_1484280600189793_5754378048447795996_n-e1792077593589.jpg)Mennon
Campbell, left, talks to Robert Sherry, who is running for reelection as Macon
city marshal (photo via Campbell campaign/Facebook)

Meredith, who considers himself a “staunch conservative,” told _Bolts_ he had
initially considered himself a Campbell supporter but was impressed with
Sharp’s conviction and ideas for the office during their podcast interview and
is now on the fence. Murray told _Bolts_ he had always enjoyed defending cases
before Judge Sharp but is backing Campbell after questioning Sharp’s judgment
on the bench in recent years. Campbell is also
[supported](https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=1482265097058010&set=a.277336547550877)
by a number of current and former sheriffs from Ouachita and Morehouse
parishes.

In some ways, Duncan said, the issues that characterized his case—especially
bite mark evidence, now roundly discredited—are relics of an earlier time,
when prosecutors were “doing whatever they wanted to people because nobody was
taking a second look.”

On the other hand, he said, the office’s continued pursuit of his case, and
the fact that many of the same figures are still involved, proves that more
needs to change.

To Duncan, new leadership at the DA’s office represents an important chance to
restore trust in the criminal legal system. Before he was wrongfully
convicted, that system was “something I used to believe in,” he told _Bolts_.
“I don’t believe [in] that anymore because I’ve seen the truth of it.”

But he hopes nonetheless that “if we have better people in office being fair
to people, and people going through the system knowing they got what they
deserve, not anything more … there's a better chance that those people are
going to go through the system and get right.”
